title: Levels of Work in School Improvement
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart distinguishes three types of school improvement work -- change, run, and serve -- and argues that most improvement efforts fail because they invest in the most visible layer (run work: meetings, CPD, planning) while neglecting serve work: the structural decisions about what is fixed vs. adaptive, who has decision authority, and how competing demands are reconciled. When serve work is underdeveloped, the system fills those gaps through individual effort rather than coherent design, producing familiar frustrations: high activity with low coherence, clear plans implemented inconsistently, monitoring that measures effort rather than meaning. Hart introduces planning for emergence as an alternative to standard improvement planning -- shifting attention upstream to the conditions that shape how people interpret and respond to the work, rather than refining action lists. The article reframes school improvement planning as system design: shaping interactions and interpretations that produce improvement rather than specifying the actions that implement it. Schools are complex systems where cause and effect are not closely related in time or space; under those conditions, coherence depends on how consistently judgment is applied across the system, not on how clearly the plan is written.
points: Change work (defining the system), run work (daily activity), and serve work (structural decisions about authority and variation) operate over different timescales and require different kinds of attention.
Serve work -- the least visible and most neglected layer -- embeds longer-term judgment into the system so others can act coherently without recreating that judgment each time.
When serve work questions are not settled deliberately, they are carried by individuals under pressure, producing inconsistency across teams even when direction is clear.
Planning for emergence shifts focus upstream from refining actions to designing the conditions that shape how people interpret and respond to the work.
In complex systems, improvement depends on how consistently judgment is applied across the system and how much variation is designed for rather than accidental -- not on plan clarity.
quotes: We define priorities, write plans, agree actions and monitor progress. It gives shape to the work and reassures us that improvement is being organised. But it does embed an assumption about where improvement sits even though it doesn't unfold in a tidy way.

At one end sits change work. This is the work of defining the system within which improvement is supposed to happen. It includes strategic intent, priorities, curriculum design, pedagogical approaches, the way we describe quality.

When these questions are not settled deliberately, they are carried by individuals, often in the moment, often under pressure and often inconsistently. Serve work shapes the conditions under which run work happens. It embeds longer term judgement into the system so that others can act coherently without having to recreate that judgement each time.

Activity can be high while improvement remains uneven. Expectations can be clear while consistency remains difficult. Monitoring can be regular without revealing the reasons behind variation. The same strategy can be introduced across a school and take hold in very different ways.
Planning for emergence means shifting attention upstream, away from refining actions and success criteria, and towards the conditions that shape how people interpret and respond to the work.

When this work is underdeveloped, the system fills the gaps itself. Teachers interpret the curriculum in different ways. Middle leaders construct their own versions of what good looks like. Teams respond to problems locally, drawing on what is available to them.
